title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 307
paragraphs: All these are customs practised by the Egyptians who dwell above the fens; and those settled in the fen-land have the same customs as the other Egyptians for the most part, both in other matters and in that each man lives with a single wife, as the Hellenes do. But for economy in food they have invented the following. When the river has become full and the plains have been flooded, there grow in the water great numbers of lilies, which the Egyptians call lotus. These they cut with a sickle and dry in the sun, and then they pound that which grows in the middle of the lotus, which is like the head of a poppy, and they make of it loaves baked with fire. The root of this lotus is also edible and has a rather sweet taste; it is round in shape and about the size of an apple. There are other lilies too, resembling roses in flower, which also grow in the river, and from them the fruit is produced in a separate vessel springing from the root beside the plant itself, and it very nearly resembles a wasp's comb. In this there grow edible seeds in great numbers, the size of an olive-stone, and they are eaten either fresh or dried. Besides this, they pull up from the fens the papyrus which grows every year, and the upper parts they cut off and put to other uses; but what is left below, for about a cubit in length, they eat or sell. Those who desire to have the papyrus at its very best bake it in an oven heated red-hot, and then eat it. Some of these people live on fish alone, drying them in the sun after having caught them and taken out the entrails, and when they are dry they use them for food.
